title: From listening to collaboration: Advancing meaningful youth engagement in rare disease research
body_markdown:
## Author


[Louise Kearney MSc Executive Director, Fortrea](https://www.fortrea.com/about-us/meet-our-team/louise-kearney-msc)


[Louise Kearney](https://www.fortrea.com/about-us/meet-our-team/louise-kearney-msc) is Head of Rare Disease, Pediatrics and Cell & Gene Therapy Strategy and Delivery at Fortrea. She has 25 years of experience across sites, biotech, pharmaceutical and CRO companies. She has worked at Fortrea for 21 years, including 10 years in Project Management and 8 years as part of the Rare Disease, Advanced Therapies and Pediatric team, where she established best practices for these complex studies. Her current role combines strategic leadership and delivery accountability for programs across the therapeutic areas within this portfolio at Fortrea. Louise acts as the central point of coordination for all CGT-related activities and workstreams.


Patient engagement has become an increasingly important part of clinical research, but when it comes to children, adolescents and young adults living with rare diseases, there remains a need for practical guidance on how to engage them in meaningful, age-appropriate ways. That is why I was pleased to contribute to the recently published paper,[Engaging Children, Adolescents and Young Adults Living With Rare Diseases as Research Partners: Practical Considerations for Meaningful Involvement](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pediatrics/articles/10.3389/fped.2026.1886270/full) , published in Frontiers in Pediatrics.


The publication was developed by the International Rare Diseases Research Consortium Working Group on Young People's Engagement and brings together perspectives from patient advocates, researchers, clinicians, industry representatives and, importantly, young people themselves. The goal was to provide practical considerations for researchers seeking to involve children and young adults as research collaborators throughout the research journey.


## Why youth engagement matters in pediatric rare disease research


Many rare diseases begin in childhood, yet young people are not always involved in decisions that directly affect them. The paper highlights how engaging young people can help shape research priorities, study design, participant materials, outcome measures and dissemination activities, leading to research that is more relevant and reflective of lived experience.


The working group also emphasizes that engagement is not a one-size-fits-all activity. Approaches should be tailored to a young person's age, developmental stage, communication needs and individual circumstances. Meaningful engagement requires researchers to move beyond simply informing participants and instead creating opportunities for consultation, collaboration and shared decision-making where appropriate.


## Best practices for engaging children and young adults in research


One of the most valuable outcomes of the publication is the development of a practical checklist to help researchers plan and implement youth engagement activities throughout the research process. The recommendations focus on creating inclusive, accessible and ethically grounded approaches that recognize young people as important contributors to research.


The paper also includes real-world examples demonstrating how youth engagement can influence pediatric clinical research. One case study features Fortrea's collaboration with the International Children's Advisory Network (iCAN) to redesign pediatric assent materials using child-friendly language and visuals. Feedback from children and caregivers helped improve comprehension and reduce anxiety, demonstrating the value of involving young people in the development of materials intended for them.


## Key takeaways for sponsors


For sponsors developing therapies for pediatric and rare disease populations, the publication offers several practical lessons:


- Engage children and young adults early in the research process to help identify barriers and opportunities before studies begin.
- Tailor engagement activities to the age, maturity, communication preferences and lived experiences of participants.
- Create opportunities for meaningful collaboration, not just feedback, allowing young people to influence decisions where appropriate.
- Design participant materials and engagement approaches that are accessible, inclusive and easy to understand.
- View patient engagement as a continuous activity that can add value throughout study design, conduct and results communication.


These recommendations reinforce an important principle: the most effective pediatric research is developed with children and families, not simply for them.


## Bringing children's voices into research


At Fortrea, we believe that effective[pediatric research](https://www.fortrea.com/therapeutics/pediatrics) starts with listening. The insights highlighted in this publication reinforce the importance of incorporating children's perspectives early and often, whether through study design reviews, patient-facing materials, assent processes or broader engagement activities. The paper concludes that embedding the perspectives, values and lived experiences of young people throughout the research process can help strengthen research outcomes and contribute to more inclusive health innovation.


As pediatric and[rare disease research](https://www.fortrea.com/therapeutics/rare-diseases) continues to evolve, meaningful engagement with children, adolescents and young adults will be increasingly important to developing studies that are feasible, participant-centered and reflective of real-world needs.


We are proud to see Fortrea represented in this important publication and grateful to all of the young people, families and organizations that continue to advocate for greater participation in research. If you are planning a pediatric or rare disease study, contact our team to discuss how we can help you create a more participant-centered research experience and support the success of your upcoming program.
